theory.overview: Passwords remain the dominant authentication method, yet storing them securely is challenging. Raw hashes fail against rainbow tables; fast hashes fail against brute force. Modern password hashing—bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2—is designed to be slow and memory-hard, making attacks prohibitively expensive even for powerful adversaries. Understanding these algorithms and their parameters is essential for anyone implementing authentication systems. A 2024 Okta breach compromised thousands of accounts because they used unsalted SHA-256 for password storage.

sections.title: Why Passwords Need Special Hashing
sections.content: Passwords are low-entropy: users choose from limited character sets and predictable patterns. A random 128-bit key has 2^128 possibilities; an 8-character password might have 2^50. Fast hashes like SHA-256 allow attackers to test billions of passwords per second on GPUs. A single RTX 4090 can compute ~14 billion SHA-256 hashes per second, cracking any 8-character password in hours. Password hashes must be slow—intentionally consuming time and memory to slow attackers while remaining usable for legitimate authentication.
keyPoints: GPUs: billions of hashes per second

sections.title: Adaptive Hashing: bcrypt
sections.content: bcrypt, designed in 1999, adapts its cost factor as hardware improves. It uses the Blowfish cipher's key schedule, iterating 2^cost times (cost typically 10-13). bcrypt includes automatic salting (22-character random salt) preventing rainbow tables. Limitations: output size fixed at 184 bits; truncates passwords over 72 bytes; memory-hardness limited. Despite age, bcrypt remains secure when cost factors are current—OWASP recommends cost 10+ minimum.

sections.title: Memory-Hard Functions: Argon2
sections.content: Argon2, winner of the Password Hashing Competition (2015), is the modern standard. It has three variants: Argon2d (fast, GPU-resistant), Argon2i (slow, side-channel resistant), Argon2id (hybrid, recommended). Argon2 takes parameters: memory size (KB), iterations, parallelism (lanes). OWASP recommends: m=47104 (46MB), t=1, p=1 for Argon2id. Memory-hardness prevents GPU attacks—GPUs have limited memory per core. Argon2 won the competition due to its tunable parameters, security proofs, and resistance to tradeoff attacks.

practiceProblems.title: Why Not SHA-256
practiceProblems.description: Why shouldn't you use SHA-256 for password hashing?

solution.answer: SHA-256 is too fast, enabling brute force attacks
solution.explanation: SHA-256 is designed to be fast. A GPU can test billions of passwords per second. Password hashing needs to be slow to limit how many passwords an attacker can test.

practiceProblems.title: Salt Purpose
practiceProblems.description: Why do we use unique salts for each password?

solution.answer: Prevent rainbow table attacks and prevent cracking multiple passwords simultaneously
solution.explanation: Without salts, attackers can precompute rainbow tables. With unique salts, each password must be cracked individually. Same passwords will have different hashes.

snippets.title: Argon2 Password Hashing
snippets.code:
import argon2

ph = argon2.PasswordHasher(time_cost=1, memory_cost=47104, parallelism=1)
hash = ph.hash('user_password')
ph.verify(hash, 'user_password')
